column1: # The recall miss table (beads tla-1sh7.3 and tla-03ep.1, epics tla-1sh7 and
# A wrong answer somebody actually writes, and what that answer says. 90 rows:
# 30 over 30 of the 120 REP rows in recall/REPS.tsv, reaching 25 of their 37
# constructs, and 60 over 38 of the 40 SPEC rows, reaching 19 of their 20.
# Rows are tab-delimited and carry the literal first field MISS, so prose in
# this file can never be read as data. Four fields, in order:
#   2  rep id       a REP or a SPEC row in recall/REPS.tsv
#   3  wrong        the wrong answer, as TLA+, verbatim
# Read rows with awk -F'\t' or cut, never with IFS=$'\t' read. Tab is an IFS
# whitespace character, so read folds a run of tabs into one delimiter.
# FIELD 4 SAYS WHAT THE WRONG ANSWER IS, NOT WHAT TO WRITE INSTEAD. The runner
# already prints both values side by side, and drill/SHEET.md already names the
# construct's syntax, so the right answer is on screen before this file speaks.
# "You wrote one function whose value at each element is the whole set" is the
# register. "You need a function set" is not.
# EVERY FIELD 3 SCORES THE WRONG-ANSWER CODE OF ITS OWN ROW KIND THROUGH
# recall/recall.sh, and each was watched doing it before its row was written:
# the REP rows on 2026-10-16 and the SPEC rows on 2026-10-17.
#   a REP row's wrong answer   rc 10  the values are not equal
#   a SPEC row's wrong answer  rc 5   every scaffold ran and the vector of
#                                     exit codes is not the one field 8 names
# An answer that scores 0 is not a miss. One that scores 150 never parsed, so
# it reports on the text rather than on the idea behind it, which is other
# feedback. On a SPEC row 75, 151 and 255 are the same class: all three are
# reachable from a wrong VARIABLES line or a wrong fairness term, and none is
# a statement about the answer, so none of them can carry a row here. That is
# why S037 and S038, the two VARIABLES reps, have no row at all: every wrong
# A SPEC ROW'S WRONG ANSWER WAS MEASURED AGAINST THE BATTERY THAT REP SHIPS,
# not against a battery that looked like it. A near neighbor can share the
# canonical's vector -- `<>(level = 1)` matched a two-sided battery and S011
# had to grow to four scaffolds -- so a row written from a guessed vector is
# a row claiming a check that does not happen.
# A REP WITH NO ROW IS THE NORMAL CASE ON THE VALUE RUNG. 90 of the 120 REP
# rows have none. A rep that finds no row here falls through to the model
# call, which is the fourth layer and is safe at this rung because the answer
# is already on screen. Padding this file to reach coverage would cost that
# THE SPEC ROWS ARE DENSER AND THE REASON IS WHAT A SPEC REP CAN SHOW. A wrong
# value gets both values side by side, which is most of the explanation before
# this file speaks. A wrong fairness condition has no value to print: what the
# runner can show is a verdict per machine. So 38 of the 40 SPEC rows carry a
# row where 30 of the 120 REP rows do.
# WHERE THE REP ROWS CAME FROM. 406 of the 498 modules under drill/*/*/verify/
# carry a leading comment naming one wrong move and what it does. Those are
# construct-level explanations wearing an item's variable names, so the work
# was re-keying them to constructs and rewriting each to name no module and no
# variable. scripts/gen-misses.sh harvests the candidates by construct. It is
# an aid and not the authority, because that rewrite is a judgment.

column3: LET Solvent(acct) == Balance[acct] > 0 IN Solvent("ann") /\ Solvent("bo")
column4: That asks for more than nothing. An account holding nothing sits at zero rather than below it, and this reads it as in the red.
That compares the whole balance against the number nothing, which is false. It's the one word fine, one word for the ledger rather than a word per account.
That asks for both at once. The train doesn't begin with wagon a, so it's false even though the half about the back of the train holds.
That asks whether both hold, and neither does. An implication whose left-hand side is false is true whatever the right-hand side says.
That says at least one account is holding something, which is true here with one account empty. It never asks about the rest.
This gives a word for the first two tracks and nothing at all for the third. A case with no arm true has no value, so there's nothing to compare.
That's a set, so it holds no order and reads the same written the other way round. Which wagon stands at the front is gone.
That's the leading wagon itself, one wagon. It's what got uncoupled, not the train left standing after it went.
That's one amount, the second. Both numbers are positions, so the second says where the run stops rather than how many to take.
That's a set with one member in it, and that member is the empty set. A box with an empty box inside isn't empty.
That's a two-member set. The first member is this yard's wagons taken as one value, so the three of them never stand alongside d.
That asks whether the two occupied tracks, taken together as one value, are themselves one of this yard's tracks. A set of two numbers isn't a number.
That counts the wagons. Two wagons on one track are two wagons and one track, so this can only agree when no track is shared.
Those are the pairs the other way round, track first. A pair is ordered, so this isn't the same collection of pairings.
That's the groups of groups, 256 of them. Every member is a set whose own members are groups of wagons, one step above a group.
That's the wagons that pass a test, and every wagon passes this one. It never says which tracks they stand on.
That's a set of truth values with at most two members. It says whether each wagon is on the third track and never which wagons those were.
That's a set holding one wagon. A set of one isn't its member, so nothing has been picked from it yet.
Colons build the set of every label with those fields. That's a set holding one label rather than the label.
That's a single entry. Its account field holds the whole set of accounts and its amount field holds the whole set of amounts.
Those are ordered pairs. Nothing in them is labeled, so the two halves are told apart by position rather than by name.
Those are the tracks the parking hands back. They're what it says, not what it has something to say about.
That's how many positions there are, a single number, rather than the positions themselves.
That's a set with one parking in it rather than the parking. An arrow between two sets builds every function across them, and here only one fits.
Those are the counts gathered loose, with nothing saying which track each one belongs to. A set has no keys to look up.
That's the whole balance with ann's entry changed, so it still says what bo holds. Its domain covers both accounts.
A merge keeps the left side on a key both sides carry, and the yard is on the left here. Wagon b stays where it was.
That's one parking, and what it gives back for every wagon is the whole set of tracks rather than a single track.
That's a parking covering wagon b alone. The other two wagons aren't held still. They've gone from the domain.
Inside the update @ is already wagon a's old track, which is a number. This applies that number as though it were a lookup.

column1: # TWELVE OF THE 37 CONSTRUCTS HAVE NO ROW, and the reasons split three ways.
# K071 RECURSIVE, K072 higher-order operator parameter, K073 LAMBDA, K075
# bracket function definition and K076 recursive function definition: the
# mistakes the drill corpus records against these do not parse. An operator
# that refers to itself with no declaration ahead of it scores 150, and so
# does a boolean expression where an operator is wanted. Measured 2026-10-16:
# LET Doubled(t) == t * 2 IN Doubled on R110 comes back 150, not 10.
# K021 LET-IN and K074 custom binary operator: value equality cannot see that
# a name was introduced, so a wrong answer against these reps is wrong about
# the body rather than about the construct. R002 carries the one row of that
# kind worth having, and it belongs to K001 for the same reason.
# K003, K005, K006, K015 and K038: I found no mistake in the drill corpus that
# these reps would catch. The near misses I tried either scored 0 against value
# equality, which means they are a correct form, or were a misreading of the
# prompt rather than a misreading of the notation.
# THE SPEC ROWS (bead tla-03ep.1). 60 wrong answers over 38 of the 40 SPEC
# reps, every one of them submitted through recall/recall.sh against the
# battery its rep ships and watched coming back rc 5 before its row was
# written. The two with no row are S037 and S038; the header says why.

column4: That promises nothing at all. With no promise a run may flip the lamp for ever, and the lift is never obliged to move.
That promises the lamp keeps flipping, which it would do anyway. The lift is the thing that can be left standing, and this says nothing about it.
That promises the machine keeps taking steps, and the lamp alone satisfies it for ever. A promise about the whole step relation says nothing about which of its parts gets a turn.
That promises the clock keeps ticking, which it does on its own. The kettle is the thing that can be left cold.
That promises something keeps happening, and the ticking is something. It never obliges the one move that runs out of work.

That is the weaker promise, and it only bites while the chance stays open without a break. The baton leaves the right hand every other moment, so the chance keeps lapsing and never taking it is allowed.
That is the weaker promise, and the signal goes red every other moment, so the chance keeps lapsing. The train is never obliged to take one of them.
That covers the tank and leaves the pump out. One run fills the tank and then flips the lamp for ever, which keeps this promise and never primes.
That promises the machine keeps moving, and the lamp keeps it moving for ever. Neither the tank nor the pump is obliged by it.
That covers the inner door and leaves the outer one shut. The buzzer can then sound for ever with the airlock half open.
That promises something keeps happening, and the buzzer is something. Neither door is obliged by it.
That promises the machine keeps moving, and the belt and the fan between them keep it moving for ever. The chute is one move of three and this names none of them.
That names a move, and the one it names is the belt, which rolls on its own. The parcels are the thing that can be left.
That promises the machine keeps moving, and rattling the drawer is moving. The queue is never obliged to go down.
That names a move, and the one it names is the drawer, which rattles on its own and serves nobody.
That claims nothing about the lift. It holds of every machine there is, the one whose lift carries on past the second floor included.
That rules out the second floor along with everything above it, so it is already false on the machine where the lift is meant to be allowed there.
That says the lamp is never lit at all. The question is about when it may be lit, not whether.
That asks for the second floor again and again rather than once. The machine that gets there and is then locked out answers the question and not this.
That asks for the lift to reach the second floor and never leave it. The question asks only that it get there.
That asks for the first floor. The express machine skips it and still reaches the top.
That asks for the second floor. The express machine goes straight there from the ground without ever calling at the first.
That asks for the second floor again and again and lets the lift leave in between. The machine that climbs and drops for ever satisfies it.
That asks for the second floor once and says nothing about staying there.
That pins the lift to one named floor rather than to being off the ground. The machine with no top stop settles above the second floor and still never returns to the ground.
That asks the lift to settle at the second floor and never leave. The machine that climbs and drops for ever reaches it again and again without ever settling.
That asks for the second floor once. However far a run has got is the part this drops.
That asks for the lamp once. The lamp that comes on and then blows satisfies it and never comes on again.
That asks for the second floor again and again whatever else is happening. The machine with the power off never lights the lamp, so the question is answered there and this is not.
That asks for the second floor once and drops the connection to the lamp altogether.
That asks for the ground again and again whatever else is happening. The machine that stops at the first floor never reaches the second, so the question is answered there and this is not.
The lift starts on the ground, so that is already true before anything has moved.
That claims nothing about any step. It holds of the machine that drops the lift as readily as of the one that does not.
That says every step which moves the lift raises it by exactly one, which is more than was asked. The express machine moves it by two and still never takes it down.

That is a claim about every state rather than about every step, and TLC checks it as an invariant rather than as a temporal property. What the two forbid here agrees; what kind of thing they are does not.
Measured against the whole state, a step that only flips the lamp is a step where the lift did not go up by one, so this is already false on the machine the question is about.
That claims nothing about any step, so it holds of the lamp that blows as readily as of the one that keeps flipping.
That says a step which touches the lamp changes it, without saying what to. The lamp that goes from lit to blown has changed and has not been turned to its other reading.
That says the lift settles at the second floor. The machine locked out on the ground can never be raised either, and its lift is nowhere near the top.
That is about the lamp, which can always be flipped, so it holds everywhere and says nothing about the lift.
That says a rise is possible again and again. The machine that never leaves the ground can always be raised and never is.
That says a step is possible again and again. The machine with the power off can always take a step that changes nothing, so something is possible for ever while nothing moves.
That claims nothing, so it holds of the machine with the power off along with every other.
That moves the lamp and holds the lift still, which is the question the other way round. The state graph is the same shape either way, so what tells them apart is which variable is meant to stay put.
That takes the lift up two floors at a time, so it reaches the second from the ground in one step and the first floor is never a state of the machine at all.
That moves the lift and holds the lamp still, which is the question the other way round.
That leaves both of them alone, so the machine has one state and nothing ever happens in it.
That leaves the whole state alone rather than the lift alone, so nothing ever happens.
That lets the lift go to any floor at all, the one below included, rather than only upwards. It reaches the same three states and generates far more steps getting there.
That is one move rather than a choice between two, and it goes up a floor at a time instead of straight to one end or the other.
That is one of the two moves rather than the relation. The lamp can then never change, so two thirds of the machine's states are out of reach.
That raises the lift and leaves the lamp where it was, so the two come apart at the first floor and the wiring between them is broken.
That turns the lamp over and leaves the lift where it was, which breaks the wiring the other way round.
That builds a run out of the rise alone, so the lamp never flips and the machine has half its states.
That is one of the two moves. The lamp then never flips, and half the machine is out of reach.
That asks for both moves in the one step, and no step can satisfy both, so the machine has an opening state and no successors.
That measures the step relation against the lift alone. Once the lift has stopped, a step that only flips the lamp leaves the subscript unchanged, so the machine counts as standing still.
That measures the step relation against the lamp alone, so on the machine where the lamp stops after one flip everything afterwards counts as standing still.
That measures the step relation against the gate alone, so once the gate has swung the ringing of the bell counts as standing still.
That measures the step relation against the bell alone, so on the machine where the bell rings once everything afterwards counts as standing still.
